stories.headline: Flights return to normal after FAA ground stop as Trump officials seek $50 billion
stories.summary: Airline schedules were returning to normal Monday after Friday's nationwide ground stop, which officials linked to a failure in the air traffic control network. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said flights were nearing full capacity. President Trump, speaking about the outage for the first time, blamed the Biden administration, and his officials asked for $50 billion for air traffic control. The FAA is preparing to brief Congress.
stories.why_it_matters: The outage stranded tens of thousands of travelers just ahead of Thanksgiving week, and whether Congress funds a faster overhaul of the aging system affects how often this can happen again.
stories.background: The Federal Aviation Administration runs the system that keeps planes safely apart in U.S. airspace, and much of it relies on decades-old equipment and telecommunications lines. On Friday, Nov. 13, the FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours after a network failure, and airlines canceled thousands more flights over the weekend as they recovered. Smaller outages, including a September failure that hit Northeast airports, had already drawn attention to the system's fragility. Congress recently gave the Transportation Department $12.5 billion for upgrades, and the administration wants more.

facts.text: The FAA grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours on Friday, and disruptions lingered through the weekend.
According to FlightAware figures cited by NPR, nearly 25,000 flights were delayed and more than 9,000 canceled on Friday.
The FAA said airline schedules were returning to normal, and officials attributed the stop to aging infrastructure and legacy technology.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said U.S. flights were nearing full capacity on Monday.

Aviation experts and federal officials told the New York Times the outage began after a new piece of networking equipment flooded the rest of the system with data; the underlying cause is still unclear.
Officials said the outage was not related to the FAA's new $875 million AI-based forecasting system, called SMART, that is being rolled out.
In his first comments on the ground stop, Trump blamed the Biden administration for the FAA's problems.
Trump administration officials asked for $50 billion for air traffic control; Congress had recently provided $12.5 billion for upgrades.
CBS News reported that audits had for years flagged billions of dollars in non-competitive FAA contracts, delays and repeated technology breakdowns.
The FAA is preparing to brief Congress on the failure.

positions.claim: A new piece of networking equipment flooded the system with data, according to experts and officials quoted by the New York Times.
Aging infrastructure and legacy technology, according to officials cited by CBS News.
Problems left by the Biden administration, according to President Trump.

stories.headline: Van Hollen says he has a path to replace Schumer as Senate Democratic leader
stories.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Sunday that his bid to lead the incoming Democratic Senate majority instead of Chuck Schumer has a "wide-open" path and is gaining support. He is calling for more inclusion within the Democratic caucus. Senate Democrats will choose their leader before the new Congress begins.
stories.why_it_matters: The Senate majority leader decides which bills and nominations get a vote, so the choice will shape what the new Democratic majority does on spending, Trump's nominees and other issues.
stories.background: Democrats won control of the Senate in this month's midterm elections, which would normally make their longtime leader, Chuck Schumer of New York, majority leader. Some Democrats, especially on the party's progressive wing, have been unhappy with Schumer's handling of fights with the Trump administration. Van Hollen, a Maryland senator, has emerged as his most prominent challenger, and Michigan's Elissa Slotkin has also been mentioned as a potential rival. Party leaders are chosen by a secret vote of the caucus.

facts.text: Van Hollen said Sunday that the race for Senate Democratic leader is "wide open" and that his challenge to Schumer is gaining support.
Van Hollen is seeking to lead the incoming Democratic majority and has called for more inclusion within the caucus.
Van Hollen said he has backing for his bid to replace Schumer.
Al-Monitor reported that Van Hollen and Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan had emerged as potential challengers to Schumer.

Uses the word "ousting," casting it as a removal of Schumer.

stories.headline: Federal prosecutor warns Sen. Warren over planned probes of Trump allies
stories.summary: Aaron Reitz, a U.S. attorney in Texas, warned Sen. Elizabeth Warren on Sunday of possible legal consequences over her plans to investigate President Trump and his associates. He demanded that she preserve documents related to her coming oversight work. With Democrats taking control of Congress, the letter sets up an early clash between the Justice Department and congressional investigators.
stories.why_it_matters: Congress's power to investigate the executive branch is a main check on government, and a federal prosecutor warning a senator about her oversight plans tests how far each branch can go against the other.
stories.background: Democrats won majorities in Congress in this month's midterms, which will give them control of committees and the power to launch investigations of the Trump administration starting in January. Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, has said she plans to investigate people close to the president. Reitz is a U.S. attorney in Texas and previously served as a senior Justice Department official under Trump. The Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause gives members of Congress broad legal protection for their legislative work, including investigations.

facts.text: U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz warned Warren on Sunday of potential legal consequences over her plans to investigate Trump and his allies and demanded she preserve related documents.
Reitz accused Warren of intending to weaponize congressional investigations, according to the Washington Times.
NBC News described Reitz as a Justice Department official warning Warren against investigating Trump associates.
Democracy Docket reported that Reitz has also sent a document-preservation demand to Sen. Richard Blumenthal over his inquiry into donors to Trump's ballroom project.

Leads with Reitz's accusation that Warren is targeting Trump associates.

coverage.takeaway: Summary only: Reitz warns of legal consequences and demands document preservation.
Headline only: highlights the weaponization accusation.

stories.headline: Judge halts Trump's plan to close a historic D.C. public golf course
stories.summary: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes on Saturday ordered a two-week pause on any work at East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, blocking its planned Sunday closure for a 15-month renovation. Trump criticized the judge and said the Interior Department will appeal. The lawsuit challenging the project continues.
stories.why_it_matters: The case tests how much control a president has over public land in the capital, and the course is Washington's most popular public golf facility.
stories.background: East Potomac Golf Links is a public course on federal parkland near the White House. The Trump administration wants to turn it into a championship-level course, and opponents sued, arguing the project bypasses legal requirements. In October, Reyes issued an injunction barring further tree removal and requiring advance notice before any closure, and the administration appealed to the D.C. Circuit. The administration had planned to close the course on Sunday.

facts.text: Judge Ana Reyes issued a temporary restraining order Saturday before the course was due to close Sunday for 15 months.
The order delays any work at the course for two weeks.
Reyes said the administration would not be responsible for operating the course while the case proceeds, according to the New York Times.
Trump said the Interior Department will appeal and called Reyes a Biden appointee; he spent the weekend posting photos of the course and called it "Trash Island."
The order is part of a months-long legal challenge to the plan to upgrade the course into a championship venue.
In late October, Reyes barred removal of more trees and required advance written notice before closing the course; the administration appealed that order.

Puts Trump's "Trash Island" nickname in the headline.

stories.headline: Trump's pick to lead the RNC faces a challenge after midterm losses
stories.summary: A rebellion is forming against Republican National Committee chairman Joe Gruters, President Trump's handpicked choice, after the party's midterm defeats. RNC co-chair KC Crosbie is challenging him, and Trump has publicly backed Gruters. The committee's 168 members will decide.
stories.why_it_matters: The national party chair controls money and rules that will shape the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, so the fight is an early test of Trump's hold on his party.
stories.background: The Republican National Committee runs the party's national fundraising, convention and nominating rules. Trump installed Joe Gruters as chairman. Republicans lost control of Congress in this month's midterm elections, which the AP described as the party's worst midterm showing in a generation. Losing parties often face internal fights over leadership afterward.

facts.text: A rebellion is forming against Trump's handpicked RNC chairman as midterm losses challenge the president's grip on the party, the AP reported.
The AP said the fight will shape the 2028 presidential nominating contest and is a rare challenge to Trump after the party's worst midterm performance in a generation.
Axios reported that RNC co-chair KC Crosbie is challenging chairman Joe Gruters, and that Trump backed Gruters on Truth Social.
The decision rests with the RNC's 168 members, according to Axios.

framing.note: Frames the challenge as a test of Trump's grip on the GOP.
Says midterm losses "test" rather than "challenge" Trump's grip, a softer wording of the same AP story.

coverage.takeaway: Headline only: the AP wire story, reprinted by ABC, PBS, the Washington Post and the Washington Times.
AP wire summary: ties the fight to the 2028 nominating race.
Headline only (paywalled): updated AP headline.

stories.headline: Lutnick faces growing scrutiny over Nvidia chip exports ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
stories.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under pressure from Republicans, Democrats and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over his handling of AI chip export controls amid the Nvidia espionage scandal. Sen. Maria Cantwell urged him to stop AI chip sales to China before Trump meets Xi Jinping this week. Reports also focus on his family's financial ties to the chipmaker.
stories.why_it_matters: Decisions on selling advanced AI chips to China affect U.S. national security and one of the country's most valuable companies, and the scandal could shape Trump's talks with Xi.
stories.background: The Commerce Department decides which advanced technology U.S. companies may sell abroad, including Nvidia's AI chips that China wants. Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned amid reports of his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and a federal investigation into a company called Megaspeed over possible chip-export violations. Lutnick, a former Wall Street executive, has been accused of taking a softer line on Nvidia than other officials. Trump is traveling to Asia this week for meetings with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

facts.text: Reports this week said Lutnick took a softer line on Nvidia over AI chip export controls, drawing pressure including from Bessent and members of Congress.
Bessent declined to defend Lutnick, according to the New York Sun.
Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO has renewed scrutiny of Lutnick, whose sons' firm has ties to the chipmaker, CNBC reported.
Sen. Maria Cantwell urged Lutnick to stop AI chip sales to China ahead of Trump's meeting with Xi.
Axios reported that Lutnick stalled Trump's planned Nvidia-related China chip curbs after Oval Office talks.
The Nvidia scandal threatens to cloud Trump's expected meeting with Xi this week, The Hill reported.

stories.headline: NTSB says tanker's steering failed before it hit a New Orleans cruise ship
stories.summary: A preliminary NTSB finding says the tanker Atlantic Asphalt suffered a steering failure that kept its rudder stuck before it crashed into the docked cruise ship American Heritage in New Orleans on Friday. Investigators recovered audio of warning whistles and emergency orders. The Port of New Orleans is suing the tanker's owners for at least $1 million.
stories.why_it_matters: The finding points investigators toward an equipment failure on a busy commercial river that passenger vessels share with large cargo ships.
stories.background: On Friday, the tanker Atlantic Asphalt struck the American Heritage riverboat-style cruise ship while it was docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans, capsizing it. Passengers, crew and two police officers ended up in the water, but no one was killed, leading to the nickname "miracle on the Mississippi." The National Transportation Safety Board investigates major transport accidents and typically takes a year or more to issue a final cause.

facts.text: The NTSB's preliminary finding is that the tanker's steering system failed, keeping its rudder in a position that sent it into the docked cruise ship.
The crash sent passengers, crew and two police officers into the Mississippi River.
The steering failed about two minutes before the collision, and investigators recovered audio and released a preliminary timeline.
The tanker's voyage recorder captured warning whistles and emergency orders before the collision.
The Port of New Orleans is seeking at least $1 million in damages from the tanker's owners; no one was killed.

framing.note: Uses the "Mississippi miracle" label and leads with the recovered audio.
Leads with the warning whistles and emergency orders.
